title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: AC9S7I01, AC9S7I02, AC9S7I03, AC9S7I04, AC9S7I05, AC9S7I06
standard_text: Develop investigable questions and hypotheses; plan safe, valid investigations, identifying variables and hazards; select equipment and record data accurately; represent data in tables and graphs; analyse patterns and errors; and evaluate methods and conclusions (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 7 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on working scientifically: hypotheses, variables, lab safety and hazard symbols, SI units, accuracy, precision, errors, graphs and evaluating investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Accurate is close to true; precise is close together.
key_sub: Control variables, repeat measurements and look for errors to make results reliable and valid.
body_html:
How to think about it

Good investigations are safe, valid and reliable.

  • State a hypothesis; change the independent variable, measure the dependent variable and control the rest.
  • Accurate results are close to the true value; precise results are close to each other. Repeats reduce random error; zeroing removes some systematic errors.
  • Graph the data (independent variable on the x-axis), find the pattern, check anomalies and evaluate the method.
Example

5.1, 5.0, 5.2 s; true value 6.0 s?

close together

far from the true value

Answer: precise but not accurate

Example

Balance reads 0.3 g when empty. Fix?

every reading is 0.3 g too high

Answer: zero (tare) it

Common mistakes

  • Confusing accuracy (close to the true value) with precision (close together).
  • Thinking more decimal places always means more accurate.
  • Including an anomalous result in the mean without checking it.

faq.q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
faq.a: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other.

faq.q: What is the difference between random and systematic errors?
faq.a: Random errors change unpredictably from one measurement to the next; repeating helps. Systematic errors shift all results the same way, such as an unzeroed balance.
It tests what it claims to test: only the independent variable changes, and all other variables are controlled.

items.q: Noah is investigating how the length of a pendulum affects the time for one swing. What is the dependent variable (the one that is measured)?
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Ethan is investigating how the height of a ramp affects the distance a toy car travels. What is the dependent variable (the one that is measured)?
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Ruby is investigating how the number of turns of wire affects the strength of an electromagnet. What is the dependent variable (the one that is measured)?
c: the number of paper clips picked up
the size of the iron nail
the number of turns of wire
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Why should a risk assessment be done before an experiment?
c: to make the results more accurate
to identify hazards and plan how to stay safe
items.e: Safety first.

items.q: Kai is investigating how the mass of a load affects the extension of a spring. What is the dependent variable (the one that is measured)?
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: William is investigating how the surface area of a container affects the rate of evaporation. What is the variable that should be kept constant?
c: the surface area of the container
the volume of water lost in a day
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: What is a hypothesis?
c: a testable explanation or prediction based on scientific ideas
items.e: Example: 'If the temperature increases, sugar will dissolve faster because particles move faster.'

items.q: Scientific knowledge sometimes changes. Why?
c: New evidence may show that an old idea needs to be improved.
items.e: This is how science progresses.

items.q: A thermometer reads 2 °C in ice water. What kind of error is this?
items.e: Pure ice water should read 0 °C.

items.q: Tom is investigating how the amount of light affects the height of bean seedlings. What is the independent variable (the one that is changed)?
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Priya is investigating how the concentration of acid affects the time for a magnesium ribbon to react. What is the variable that should be kept constant?
c: the time for the magnesium to disappear
the length of the magnesium ribbon
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Why should the air hole of a Bunsen burner be closed when it is lit?
c: to get a visible yellow safety flame
items.e: The safety flame is easy to see when the burner is not in use.

items.q: Why must you wear safety goggles when heating chemicals?
c: to protect your eyes from splashes and hot chemicals
to see the flame more clearly
items.e: Goggles protect against splashes.

items.q: Harper is investigating how the surface area of a container affects the rate of evaporation. What is the independent variable (the one that is changed)?
c: the surface area of the container
the volume of water lost in a day
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Tom is investigating how the temperature of water affects the time for sugar to dissolve. What is the variable that should be kept constant?
c: the time for the sugar to dissolve
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Which Bunsen burner flame is used for heating?
c: the blue non-luminous flame, with the air hole open
the yellow luminous flame, with the air hole closed
a flame with the gas turned off
items.e: The blue flame is hotter and does not leave soot.

items.q: What does 'accurate' mean for a measurement?
items.e: Accuracy is about closeness to the true value.

items.q: Tom is investigating how the concentration of acid affects the time for a magnesium ribbon to react. What is the dependent variable (the one that is measured)?
c: the time for the magnesium to disappear
the length of the magnesium ribbon
items.e: Independent: changed. Dependent: measured. Controlled: kept the same so the test is fair.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The lamp glowed brighter with two batteries.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “Salt makes iron rust faster.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: What is the SI unit of length?
items.e: The SI unit of length is the metre (m).

items.q: What is an evaporating dish used for?
c: To hold a hot test tube.
To hold and heat liquids (it gives only a rough volume).
To evaporate a solution to get the solid.
To hold liquids that are swirled, so they do not splash out.
items.e: An evaporating dish is used to evaporate a solution to get the solid.

items.q: What is the SI unit of energy?
items.e: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J).

items.q: Which statement is a conclusion rather than an observation?
c: Sugar dissolves faster in hotter water.
There were crystals at the bottom.
The water turned clear after 30 s.
items.e: A conclusion explains a pattern in the results.

items.q: What is the SI unit of mass?
items.e: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

items.q: Which apparatus is used to support a beaker over a Bunsen burner?
c: a tripod stand and wire gauze
items.e: A tripod stand and wire gauze is used to support a beaker over a Bunsen burner.

items.q: What is a conical flask used for?
c: To transfer a fixed volume of liquid accurately.
To add a liquid drop by drop and measure the volume added accurately.
To hold liquids that are swirled, so they do not splash out.
items.e: A conical flask is used to hold liquids that are swirled, so they do not splash out.

items.q: What is the SI unit of volume?
items.e: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre (m³).

items.q: What is an electronic balance used for?
c: To measure the volume of a liquid.
items.e: An electronic balance is used to measure mass.

items.q: Which hazard label is most suitable for ethanol?
items.e: Ethanol catches fire easily.

items.q: Which apparatus is used to measure time?
c: a retort stand with a clamp
a tripod stand and wire gauze
items.e: A stopwatch is used to measure time.

items.q: Which hazard label is most suitable for hydrogen peroxide?
items.e: Hydrogen peroxide provides oxygen and makes other substances burn more fiercely.

items.q: Which hazard label is most suitable for concentrated sulfuric acid?
items.e: Concentrated sulfuric acid destroys living tissue and some materials on contact.

items.q: Which apparatus is used to hold apparatus firmly in place?
c: a retort stand with a clamp
items.e: A retort stand with a clamp is used to hold apparatus firmly in place.

items.q: What does the hazard symbol for a harmful or irritant substance warn you about?
c: The substance may explode when heated, struck or exposed to a flame.
The substance provides oxygen and makes other substances burn more fiercely.
The substance can cause redness or blisters on the skin, or is less dangerous than toxic.
The substance can cause death or serious harm if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through the skin.
items.e: This is the meaning of the harmful or irritant symbol.

items.q: What does the hazard symbol for an explosive substance warn you about?
c: The substance provides oxygen and makes other substances burn more fiercely.
The substance can cause redness or blisters on the skin, or is less dangerous than toxic.
The substance may explode when heated, struck or exposed to a flame.
items.e: This is the meaning of the explosive symbol.

items.q: A student timed 10 swings of a pendulum as 15.2 s. What is the time for one swing?
items.e: Timing many swings and dividing reduces the error.

items.q: Which apparatus is used to add a liquid drop by drop and measure the volume added accurately?
items.e: A burette is used to add a liquid drop by drop and measure the volume added accurately.

items.q: What is a thermometer used for?
c: To hold and heat liquids (it gives only a rough volume).
To support a beaker over a Bunsen burner.
To hold apparatus firmly in place.
items.e: A thermometer is used to measure temperature.

items.q: Which hazard label is most suitable for mercury?
items.e: Mercury can cause death or serious harm if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through the skin.

items.q: A student measured the height of bean seedlings after 10 days four times: 2.6 cm, 4.7 cm, 2.8 cm, 2.9 cm. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
items.e: The anomaly is 4.7 cm. Mean of the other three: 8.3 ÷ 3 = 2.8 cm.

items.q: A student measured the time for a trolley to roll down a ramp four times: 3.2 s, 3.3 s, 3.1 s, 5.2 s. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
items.e: The anomaly is 5.2 s. Mean of the other three: 9.6 ÷ 3 = 3.2 s.

items.q: Mia's four results are 5.1 s, 5.0 s, 5.2 s and 5.1 s. The true value is 6.0 s. How would you describe them?
items.e: They agree closely but are far from the true value.

items.q: Which change makes an investigation more valid?
c: using brighter colours on the graph
controlling all variables except the one being tested
items.e: Validity is about a fair test.

items.q: Ella says her conclusion is proven because one test worked. What is wrong?
c: One test is not enough; results must be repeated and checked.
items.e: Science gathers evidence over many tests.

items.q: Why should long hair be tied back in the laboratory?
c: so that it does not catch fire or fall into chemicals
items.e: Safety first near flames.

items.q: What should you do first if a chemical splashes on your skin?
c: Wash it with plenty of running water and tell the teacher.
Wipe it with paper and continue.
items.e: Report every accident.

items.q: What is the purpose of a control set-up in an experiment?
c: to compare with the experimental set-up, to show that the change is caused by the variable tested
items.e: For example, a set-up without light when testing the effect of light.

items.q: What is a systematic error?
c: an error that shifts every result in the same way, such as a balance not zeroed
items.e: Repeats do not remove systematic errors.

items.q: A student repeats an experiment three times: 24 s, 25 s, 41 s. What should she do?
c: treat 41 s as anomalous, repeat it, and average the reliable results
items.e: Anomalous results do not fit the pattern.

items.q: Which variable goes on the x-axis of a line graph?
items.e: The dependent variable goes on the y-axis.

items.q: What is a random error?
c: a broken thermometer reading 2 °C too high
unpredictable variation, such as reaction time when using a stopwatch
items.e: Repeats reduce the effect of random errors.

items.q: Ruby tests if fertiliser affects plant growth using 2 plants. How could she improve reliability?
c: use more plants in each group and repeat
items.e: Larger samples are more reliable.

items.q: What is a valid investigation?
c: one that gives the expected result
one that tests what it is meant to test, with other variables controlled
items.e: Valid means it answers the question fairly.

items.q: Which measurement is most precise?
items.e: Precision depends on the smallest division used.

items.q: Why do scientists repeat measurements and calculate a mean?
c: to reduce the effect of random errors and improve reliability
because one result is always wrong
items.e: Repeats show whether results are consistent.

items.q: A student measured the temperature rise of water heated for 2 minutes four times: 2.9 °C, 5.1 °C, 3.3 °C, 3.1 °C. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
items.e: The anomaly is 5.1 °C. Mean of the other three: 9.3 ÷ 3 = 3.1 °C.

items.q: A student measured the distance a paper plane flew four times: 6.1 m, 6 m, 4.4 m, 5.9 m. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
items.e: The anomaly is 4.4 m. Mean of the other three: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 m.

items.q: What is the SI unit of force?
items.e: The SI unit of force is the newton (N).

items.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
items.e: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the amount of rain in each month of the year?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Distance a toy car rolls from different ramp heights. What pattern does the graph show?
c: As the ramp height increases, the distance increases.
As the ramp height increases, the distance decreases.
items.e: Follow the line from left to right.

items.q: Distance a toy car rolls from different ramp heights. At which ramp height was the value 180 cm?
items.e: Find 180 cm on the side axis, go across to the line, then down.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The nail in salt water had the most rust after a week.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Temperature of water in a black bottle in the sun. What is the value when the time is 10?
items.e: Go up from 10 on the bottom axis to the line, then across.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “Slaters prefer the dark because it is safer from birds.”

c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Height of a sunflower. What pattern does the graph show?
c: As the week increases, the height decreases.
As the week increases, the height increases.
items.e: Follow the line from left to right.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the temperature of cooling water every 2 minutes?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the number of each kind of bird seen at a waterhole?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the number of students who walk, ride or drive to school?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the favourite fruit of students in a class?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Temperature of a cup of tea cooling. What is the value when the time is 15?
items.e: Go up from 15 on the bottom axis to the line, then across.

items.q: How should you read the volume of water in a measuring cylinder?
c: from above, at the top of the meniscus
at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus
items.e: This avoids parallax error.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The water in the black bottle reached 40 °C.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Why should only one variable be changed in a fair test?
c: so the results are always the same
so that any change in the results is caused by that variable only
items.e: All other variables are kept constant.

items.q: Temperature of a cup of tea cooling. What pattern does the graph show?
c: As the time increases, the temperature decreases.
As the time increases, the temperature increases.
items.e: Follow the line from left to right.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing which of four materials kept ice frozen longest?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: When heating a liquid in a test tube, where should you point the mouth of the tube?
c: away from yourself and other people
items.e: Hot liquid may spurt out.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “Wool traps air, so it slows down heat moving into the ice.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The ice cube wrapped in wool took 52 minutes to melt.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: What is a hypothesis?
c: a fact that can never change
a possible explanation that can be tested by an experiment
items.e: For example: 'Sugar dissolves faster in hot water because particles move faster.'

items.q: Which graph is best for showing the temperature in Alice Springs every hour for a day?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: What does the hazard symbol for an oxidising substance warn you about?
c: The substance provides oxygen and makes other substances burn more fiercely.
The substance can cause redness or blisters on the skin, or is less dangerous than toxic.
The substance can cause death or serious harm if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through the skin.
The substance destroys living tissue and some materials on contact.
items.e: This is the meaning of the oxidising symbol.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The seedling grew tall and pale because it was looking for light.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Noah uses a stopwatch to time a ball falling 1 m. Why are his times so variable?
c: Human reaction time adds random error to short times.
items.e: Use a longer fall or a light gate.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The seedling in the cupboard was pale and 9 cm tall.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: What does the hazard symbol for a corrosive substance warn you about?
c: The substance can cause death or serious harm if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through the skin.
The substance may explode when heated, struck or exposed to a flame.
The substance destroys living tissue and some materials on contact.
items.e: This is the meaning of the corrosive symbol.

items.e: Go up from 3 on the bottom axis to the line, then across.

items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: A class measures the boiling point of water as 98 °C, 99 °C and 98 °C. Why might this differ from 100 °C?
c: Boiling point changes every day for no reason.
Air pressure, impurities or thermometer error can change the reading.
items.e: Look for sources of error.

items.q: Temperature of water in a black bottle in the sun. What pattern does the graph show?
c: As the time increases, the temperature decreases.
As the time increases, the temperature increases.
items.e: Follow the line from left to right.

items.q: Jack's balance reads 0.3 g with nothing on it. What should he do?
items.e: This removes a systematic error.

items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.e: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen may explode when heated, struck or exposed to a flame.

The substance can cause redness or blisters on the skin, or is less dangerous than toxic.
The substance may explode when heated, struck or exposed to a flame.

items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Which graph is best for showing how far a car rolls from ramps of different heights?
items.e: Use a column graph for separate groups and a line graph when both variables are numbers that change.

items.q: Why do scientists publish their methods in detail?
c: so others can repeat the investigation and check the results
items.e: Reproducibility builds trust in results.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “18 of the 20 slaters moved to the dark side.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.
